item.title: Ben Brody || Artist Talk — Wed Sep 16, 1:30 PM — Center for Documentary Studies
item.description:
With the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, photographer Ben Brody will present his work documenting and interpreting the wars that followed. Working at the intersection of photojournalism, art, and propaganda, Brody spent more than 13 years photographing in Iraq and Afghanistan, first as an enlisted soldier and later as an independent photojournalist. His published photobooks explore the culture of information warfare used to sell the so-called Global War on Terror, and the struggle of its combatants to make sense of it.
This talk will be held at the Center for Documentary Studies auditorium, 1317 W. Pettigrew Street. Street parking is available.
Bio: Ben Brody is an independent photographer, educator, and picture editor working on long-form projects related to the American wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and their aftermath. He is the Director of Photography for Report for America, and a co-founder of Mass Books.

item.title: Physics Colloquium - Reverse Physics: From Laws to Physical Assumptions — Wed Sep 16, 3:30 PM — None
item.description: When the math is derived from the right physical assumptions, the physical assumptions can be derived from the math. item.title: Population-Environment: From Challenges to Win-Win Solutions? — Thu Sep 17, 12:00 PM — SSRI-Gross Hall 270
item.description:
How do human populations impact the environment and how do they respond to environmental change? This talk presents recent research examining how aspects of human population and dynamics impact the environment and, in turn, how they respond to environmental change. Research is presented from rural regions in Latin America, Africa, Asia, and California. Population has long played a key role in environmental change; the environment, in turn, has long impacted human population. However, we still lack an overarching theory of population-environment dynamics. Towards filling this gap, the presentation features case studies, qualitative and quantitative methods, and primary data and secondary data. Analytical methods are largely statistical models with complementary qualitative analyses. Results suggest significant roles that population play directly and indirectly on environmental dynamics and various forms of human population responses to environmental change.
Source: Duke University

Drawing on examples from research, practice, evaluation, and policy, nurse scientist Kelli DePriest, PhD, RN, will examine how community health nurses can use data-driven insights, place-based perspectives, and cross-sector collaborations to better understand and respond to population health challenges. Participants will gain a deeper appreciation for community health nursing as an expansive and analytic field and identify strategies to strengthen the profession through education, investment, leadership, and collaborative action.

item.title: Teen Science Café: Unwinding Spiral Galaxies — Fri Oct 2, 6:00 PM — Downtown Raleigh
item.description:
The winding arms of spiral galaxies are one of their most obvious features. By measuring how tightly the arms are wrapped, we can reveal clues about other components that are much harder to observe, such as dark matter content and central black hole mass. We aim to partner volunteers with AI in order to identify individual spiral arms in tens of thousands of galaxies, measure how tightly each arm is wound, and use those measurements to estimate these elusive properties. Doing so will help us better understand how galaxies similar to our own Milky Way form and evolve.
About the Presenter Dr. Patrick Treuthardt is the Assistant Head of the Astronomy & Astrophysics Research Lab at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences and a Research Affiliate in the Department of Computing Sciences at Coastal Carolina University. Certified mindfulness meditation teacher Barbara Shumannfang will guide a variety of meditations for you to try, ending with tips on how to apply mindfulness in your daily life. Remember to bring water to drink, bug spray (there will be bugs, and we’ll be walking very slowly and stopping at times), and a towel/lightweight seat to sit on along the way. If the ground is damp, we will provide individual tarps for sitting. The trail is mostly flat and includes a couple of steps up and down from a boardwalk, as well as sections with tree roots. item.title: History for Lunch: Thomas Day – Cabinetmaker and Free Person of Color — Wed Oct 7, 12:00 PM — Museum of the Albemarle
item.description:
Thomas Day was a freeborn Black artisan renowned for his work in North Carolina and Virginia. Known as an enslaver with ties to northern abolitionists and the American Colonization Society, Day illustrates the moral complexities of life in pre-Civil War North Carolina. In this presentation, Assistant Site Manager David Rayburn of Thomas Day State Historic Site will discuss Day's contradictory life and the research conducted since his home and workshop were acquired by the State of North Carolina in 2024.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

Crabtree will explore the role public broadcast television plans in telling visual stories rooted in state and national history. Hosted by North Carolina-based podcaster Michael A. Betts II, the discussion will spotlight shows such as NC Weekend, which features historic revolutionary sites across the state, as well as the nationally acclaimed Ken Burns series, The American Revolution, in which Carolina's own Katlhleen DuVal is featured prominently. The conversation will highlight the power of documentary film and television as an educational tool to engage citizens across the state and nation in our collective story.

item.title: Seeing the Garden — Plein Air Landscape Painting Through Observation — Wed Oct 21, 9:30 AM — Duke Gardens–Barnes Welcome Center
item.description: “Seeing the Garden” is a painting class with instructor James Keul, Durham-based artist and avid gardener, focused on direct observation of the cultivated landscape at Duke Gardens. Working in watercolor, students will interpret light, atmosphere, color and spatial design through careful study of the natural environment. The class emphasizes slow looking and close observation, encouraging students to experience the gardens not only as visitors, but as artists interpreting a living landscape. Participants will explore how pathways, plantings, seasonal color, water and architectural elements create visual rhythm and composition within the garden. Through an instructor demonstration, short studies and a guided painting session, students will develop practical plein air painting skills while deepening their appreciation for horticulture, ecology and landscape design.
